source_text: Hunc ergo, omissis haereticorum fabulis atque figmentis, deum nouit et ueneratur ecclesia; cui testimonium reddit tam inuisibilium quam etiam uisibilium et semper et tota natura: quem angeli adorant, astra mirantur, maria benedicunt, terrae uerentur, inferna quaeque suspiciunt: quem mens omnis humana sentit, etiam si non exprimit: cuius imperio omnia commouentur, fontes scaturiunt, amnes labuntur, fluctus assurgunt, fetus suos cuncta parturiunt, uenti spirare coguntur, imbres ueniunt, maria commouentur, fecunditates suas cuncta ubique diffundunt. qui peculiarem protoplastis aeternae uitae mundum quendam paradisum in oriente constituit: avdorem uitae plantauit; scientiae boni et mai similiter alteram arborem collocauit; mandatum dedit; sententiam contra delictum statuit; Noe iustissimum de diluui periculis pro merito innocentiae fideique seruauit; Enoch transtulit; in amicitiae societatem Abraham allegit; Isaac protexit; Iacob auxit; Moysen ducem populo praefecit; ingemiscentes filios Israel e iugo seruitutis eripuit; legem scripsit; patrum subolem in terram repromissionis induxit; prophetas spiritu instruxit; et per hos omnes filium suum Christum repromisit; et quando daturum se spoponderat, misit. per quem nobis in notitiam uenire uoluit, et in nos indulgentiae suae sinus largos profudit, egenis et abiectis locupletem spiritum conferendo. et quia ultro et largus et bonus est, ne totus hic orbis auersus gratiae eius fluminibus aresceret, apostolos institutores generis nostri in totum orbem mitti per filium suum uoluit, ut condicio generis humani agnosceret institutorem, et, si sequi maluisset, haberet quem pro deo in suis iam postulationibus patrem diceret. cuius non prouidentia tantummodo singillatim per homines cucurrit aut currit, sed etiam per ipsas urbes et ciuitates, quarum exitus prophetarum uocibus cecinit; immo etiam per ipsum totum orbem, cuius propter incredulitatem exitus, plagas, deminutiones poenasque descripsit. et ne quis non etiam ad minima quaeque dei putaret istam infatigabilem prouidentiam peruenire, ex duobus, inquit dominus, passeribus unus non cadet sine patris uoluntate, sed et capilli capitis uestri omnes numerati sunt; cuius etiam cura et prouidentia Israelitarum non siuit nec uestes consumi, nec uilissima iz pedibus calciamenta deteri, sed nec ipsorum postremum adulescentium captiua sarabara comburi. nec immerito; nam si hic omnia complexus est omnia continens (omnia autem et totum ex singulis constant), pertinget consequenter eius ad usque singula quaeque cura, cuius ad totum, quicquid est, peruenit prouidentia. Hinc est quod et desuper cherubim sedet, id est, praeest super operum suorum uarietatem, subiectis throno eius animalibus prae ceteris principatum tenentibus, cuncta desuper crystallo contegente, id est, caelo omnia operiente: quod in firmamentum de aquarum fluente materia fuerat deo iubente solidatum, ut glacies robusta aquarum terram pridem contegentium diuidens medietatem dorso quodam pondera aquae superioris, corroboratis de gelu uiribus, sustineret. nam et rotae subiacent, tempora scilicet, quibus omnia semper mundi membra uoluuntur talibus pedibus adiectis, quibus non in perpetuum stant ista, sed transeunt. sed et per omnes artus stellata sunt oculis; dei enim opera peruigili obtutu contemplanda sunt. in quorum sinu carbonum medius est ignis; siue quoniam ad igneum diem iudicii mundus iste festinat; siue quoniam omnia opera dei ignea, nec sunt tenebrosa, sed uigent; siue etiam, ne, quia ex terrenis ista fuerant orta principiis, naturaliter de originis suae rigore torperent, addita est omnibus interioris spiritus calida natura, quae frigidis concreta corporibus ad usuram uitae aequalia omnibus libramenta ministraret. hic est igitur currus, secundum Dauid, dei. currus enim, inquit, dei decies milies multtMultiplicatus, id est, innumerus, infinitus, immensus. — sub iugo enim naturalis legis omnibus datae alia quasi frenis reuocata retrahuntur, alia quasi effusis habenis excitata impelluntur. mundum enim istum currum dei cum omnibus et ipsi angeli ducunt et astra; quorum uarios licet meatus, certis tamen legibus uinctos, inspicimus ad metas definiti sibi temporis ducere; ut merito nobis quoque cum apostolo et artificem et opera mirantibus exclamare iam libeat: altitudo diuttiarum sapientiae et scientiae dei, quam inscrutabilia iudicia eius et inuestigabiles uiae eius et reliqua.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore, the Church knows and venerates this God, omitting the fables and figments of heretics; to whom testimony is rendered by both invisible and visible things, and by the whole of nature always; whom angels adore, stars marvel at, seas bless, lands reverence, and all things in hell look up to; whom every human mind perceives, even if it does not express it; by whose command all things are moved, fountains gush forth, rivers flow, waves surge, all things give birth to their offspring, winds are forced to breathe, rains come, seas are moved, and all things everywhere diffuse their fertility. Who established a certain paradise, a world of eternal life, in the east for the first-formed humans; planted the tree of life; similarly placed another tree of knowledge of good and evil; gave a command; established a sentence against sin; saved Noah, the most just, from the dangers of the flood on account of his innocence and faith; transferred Enoch; chose Abraham into the fellowship of friendship; protected Isaac; increased Jacob; appointed Moses as leader of the people; rescued the groaning sons of Israel from the yoke of servitude; wrote the law; led the offspring of the fathers into the land of promise; instructed prophets with the Spirit; and through all these promised his Son Christ; and when he had promised to give him, he sent him. Through whom he wished us to come into knowledge, and poured out the large bosom of his indulgence upon us, conferring a rich Spirit upon the needy and the cast out. And because he is spontaneous, generous, and good, he did not want this whole world to dry up, turned away from the streams of his grace, and therefore he wanted apostles, the instructors of our race, to be sent into the whole world through his Son, so that the condition of the human race might recognize its instructor, and, if it wished to follow, might have someone to call Father in its prayers. Whose providence not only runs or has run through individual humans, but also through the cities and states themselves, whose outcomes the prophets have sung; indeed, even through the whole world, whose outcome, plagues, diminutions, and punishments he has described on account of its unbelief. And lest anyone think that this untiring providence of God does not reach even the smallest things, the Lord says: not one of two sparrows falls without the will of the Father, but even the hairs of your head are all numbered; whose care and providence did not allow the clothes of the Israelites to wear out, nor their sandals, the most worthless things, to deteriorate, nor even the captives' hair to be burned. Not without reason; for if he has encompassed all things, containing all things (and all things and the whole consist of individual things), consequently his care reaches to each individual thing, whose providence extends to the whole, whatever it is. Hence it is that he sits upon the cherubim, that is, he presides over the variety of his works, with animals subject to his throne, holding principality over the rest, and all things covered with crystal above, that is, with heaven operating over all things; which was solidified in the firmament from the flowing matter of the waters by God's command, so that the robust ice of the waters, dividing the upper and lower parts, might sustain the weight of the upper waters with its strengthened forces. For the wheels are also underneath, namely the times, by which all the members of the world are always turned, with feet added to them, by which these things do not stand forever, but pass away. But also, through all the parts, they are studded with starry eyes; for the works of God are to be contemplated with a wakeful gaze. In whose midst is the fire of the coals; either because this world hastens to the fiery day of judgment; or because all the works of God are fiery, and not dark, but vigorous; or also, lest, because these things arose from earthly principles, they might naturally grow cold from the rigor of their origin, the warm nature of the inner Spirit has been added to all things, which might minister equal balances to all the frozen bodies for the use of life. This, therefore, is the chariot of God, according to David. For he says: the chariot of God is multiplied ten thousand times, that is, innumerable, infinite, immense. — For under the yoke of the natural law, all things have been given, and some are restrained as if with reins, while others are impelled as if with loosened reins. For the angels and the stars lead this world, the chariot of God, with all its parts; whose varied courses, though bound by certain laws, we see leading to the goals of a defined time; so that we also, with the apostle, marveling at the artisan and his works, may now exclaim: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how unsearchable are his judgments and his ways inscrutable, and the rest.

pass_b_english: The Church knows and venerates this God, setting aside the fables and fabrications of heretics; all creation — invisible and visible alike, the whole of nature at all times — bears witness to him. Angels adore him, the stars marvel, the seas bless him, the lands reverence him, and everything in the netherworld looks up to him. Every human mind perceives him, even if it cannot put that perception into words. By his command all things are set in motion: fountains gush, rivers flow, waves surge, every creature brings forth its young, winds are compelled to blow, rains fall, seas are stirred, and everywhere fertility spreads abroad.

He planted a paradise in the east, a world of eternal life, for the first-formed humans; he set there the tree of life and likewise the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; he gave a command and fixed a penalty for transgression. He saved Noah, the most just, from the flood because of his innocence and faith; he transferred Enoch; he brought Abraham into the fellowship of friendship; he protected Isaac and increased Jacob; he appointed Moses to lead the people; he rescued the groaning sons of Israel from the yoke of slavery; he wrote the Law; he led the fathers' offspring into the promised land; he instructed the prophets by the Spirit; and through them all he promised his Son Christ — and when the time came to give him, he sent him.

Through the Son he willed us to come to knowledge of him, and he poured out the broad bosom of his mercy upon us, conferring a rich Spirit on the needy and the outcast. Because he is generous, bountiful, and good, he did not want the whole world to wither, cut off from the streams of his grace. So he willed that apostles, instructors of our race, be sent into all the world through his Son, that the human condition might recognize its teacher and, if it chose to follow, have someone to call Father in its prayers (Psalm 68:17).

His providence does not merely run through individual lives; it runs through cities and nations, whose destinies the prophets have sung — indeed, through the whole world, whose end, plagues, diminutions, and punishments he has foretold because of its unbelief. Lest anyone imagine this untiring providence fails to reach the smallest details, the Lord says: not one of two sparrows falls without the Father's will, and even the hairs of your head are all numbered. His care did not allow the Israelites' clothing to wear out, nor their sandals — the lowliest things — to deteriorate, nor even the captives' hair to be burned. There is good reason: if he embraces all things and contains all things (for the whole and all things consist of individual parts), then his care inevitably extends to each single thing, since his providence already reaches the whole, whatever it is.

Therefore he sits upon the cherubim — that is, he presides over the variety of his works, with the living creatures subject to his throne holding first place among the rest, and all things covered overhead by the crystal firmament, which is heaven covering all. At God's command this firmament was solidified from the flowing substance of the waters into robust ice, dividing the upper and lower waters so that, its strength reinforced by frost, it could bear the weight of the upper waters. Beneath it turn the wheels — that is, the times — by which all the members of the world are continually revolved; feet are added to them so that these things do not stand forever but pass away. And through every part they are studded with starry eyes, for God's works are to be contemplated with a wakeful gaze. In their midst is the fire of coals: either because this world hastens toward the fiery day of judgment, or because all God's works are fiery, not dark but vigorous, or lest, having arisen from earthly principles, they might naturally grow cold from the rigor of their origin — so the warm nature of the inner Spirit was added to all things to supply equal balances for the use of life to bodies frozen by cold.

This, then, is the chariot of God, according to David: 'The chariot of God is multiplied ten thousand times,' that is, innumerable, infinite, immense. Under the yoke of the natural law given to all, some are drawn back as with reins, others driven forward as with loosened reins. The angels and the stars guide this world, the chariot of God, with all its parts; their varied courses, though bound by fixed laws, we see leading to the goals of an appointed time — so that we too, with the apostle, marveling at the artisan and his work, may rightly exclaim: O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and his ways inscrutable, and all that follows.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological and cosmological descriptions in the Latin text. Scripture citations (Matthew 10:29-30/Luke 12:6-7 alluded to in the sparrow/hair passage, and the Psalm reference) are handled correctly. Pass A and B are consistent with the Latin source.
